The appeal concerns the conviction of the accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for murder, with the prosecution required to establish the offence beyond reasonable doubt before the evidential burden shifts to the accused under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act. The judgment reaffirmed that the shift of burden is applicable only after the prosecution’s case meets the requisite standard, and the appeal was disposed of.

The Court reiterated that compliance with the two‑witness requirement establishes execution, but execution alone does not conclusively prove the Will’s legal effect without satisfying the evidentiary examination stipulated by Section 68.

document.case_note_ai: The appeal concerns the grant of bail in a murder case (Section 302 IPC) where the accused were also alleged to have committed offences under Section 135 of the Maharashtra Police Act and the Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act (MCOCA), particularly the stringent bail bar in Section 21(4) MCOCA. The central issue is whether the trial court could exercise its discretion under Section 439 of the CrPC to grant bail despite the rigour of Section 21(4) MCOCA and the provisions of Section 135 Maharashtra Police Act. The court held that the constitutional power to grant bail is not ousted by such specific statutory restrictions and may be exercised if the circumstances justify it. Accordingly, bail was granted to the respondents, affirming the principle that stringent bail provisions do not override the court’s inherent jurisdiction to release an accused on bail.
